that I tasted the soup before adding the pepper. This is exactly the same mentality that we need to use when we're building curricular interactions.
We want students getting their "tastes" before they add their own spices. That extra gravy that I added to my soup is developed by my students through reading, writing, and collaborating.
Students can work on putting it all together after they've had the chance to get a true taste of what is expected of them. And that is powerful! There is tremendous buy-in when students have been given large amounts of choice in crafting their curricular products.
There is no one way to make soup. And, I beieve, there should NOT be one way to put an entire curricular season together. The skills, strategies, and talents of our students are continuously changing. So, the experiences and products that students make should evolve with them as well.
To use another analogy, every year I am introduced to some new, fun "Waldorf Salad." The vegetables remain the same (for consistency), but there is a new dressing that makes the experience fresh!
***
As I think back on my most favorite kinds of soup, I consider that I have a celeriac and apple soup so I can taste the finesse of change. But, mostly, I enjoy a good old-fashined vegetable soup, without too many changes to its essence. Its very basic core.
Every year I try a new curriculum. I make huge adjustments and alterations, and my students still deeply satisfy my need to fill my learning stomach.
This is because the "meat" of any curriculum is authentic literacy lessons and exploration. My job as a Literacy Specialist is the same every year, but its how I get to the students that are different. The curriculum and my approach is always fresh, but the fundamentals of my work stay the same.
